false_positives.candidate:
Changing span-buffer keys from sets to sorted sets breaks rolling deploys

Existing `span-buf:s:*` keys in Redis were written as sets by the previous `SADD`/`SSCAN` implementation. After a rolling deploy those keys can remain for the Redis TTL (default 3600s) and are still referenced by the flush queue, but the new code performs `ZADD` here and `ZSCAN`/`ZCARD`/`ZUNIONSTORE` elsewhere on them. Redis raises `WRONGTYPE Operation against a key holding the wrong kind of value`, so consumers and flushers fail and buffered spans can be lost. This needs a versioned key prefix, backward-compatible handling, or draining the buffer before deploy.

ZUNIONSTORE default SUM corrupts eviction scores for duplicate spans

`ZUNIONSTORE` without an aggregate uses `SUM`. Span processing is at-least-once, so after a span has been merged into a parent set, a retry can re-add the same payload to the source key; when the sets are merged again the member exists in both destination and source and its score is doubled. The score is `end_timestamp_precise`, so the `ZPOPMIN` eviction ordering is corrupted (an old span can look newer and survive eviction). The merge should preserve the original timestamp, e.g. with `AGGREGATE MAX`.

Eviction cap hardcodes 1000 and ignores max_segment_spans

The new eviction limit is hard-coded to 1000, while `SpansBuffer` still accepts `max_segment_spans` (default 1001) but no longer uses it. Deployments that configure a different limit are silently ignored, and spans beyond 1000 are dropped without any metric or log because the previous `segment_span_count_exceeded` signal was removed. This changes the configured data-loss boundary without visibility.

Redirect loop cap lowered to 1000 can misroute deep traces

The redirect-resolution loop was reduced from 10000 to 1000 iterations and the comment documenting the depth limitation was removed. For a project/trace chain longer than 1000 parent links, the loop stops at an intermediate span and writes the redirect to the wrong set, so spans can be merged into the wrong segment or split across segments. The redirect hash is not bounded by the 1000-span eviction cap until flush.

No test exercises the new eviction behavior

All test changes only add the new required `end_timestamp_precise` field to existing fixtures. There is no test that inserts more than 1000 spans to exercise the new `ZPOPMIN` cap, verifies that the oldest spans are evicted, or checks sorted-set merge behavior for duplicate payloads/scores. The main behavior added by this PR is therefore untested.

false_positives.candidate:
Accidental submodule/gitlink `sentry-repo` committed at PR base commit

The PR adds a file `sentry-repo` whose only content is `Subproject commit a5d290951def84afdcc4c88d2f1f20023fc36e2a` (the PR base SHA), with no corresponding `.gitmodules` entry in the change. This is a gitlink to a nested repository checkout, almost certainly committed by accident. Checking it in makes the tree contain a broken/uninitialized submodule reference that can confuse CI, `git submodule` tooling, and clean checkouts. It is unrelated to the feature and should be removed before merge.

`_is_error_focused_query` substring match matches negated and mixed queries

`_is_error_focused_query` returns True whenever the raw query string contains the substring `event.type:error`, using `'event.type:error' in query`. That is true for negated filters such as `!event.type:error` (which selects transactions) and for mixed clauses such as `event.type:error OR event.type:transaction`. In those cases upsampling is enabled and `count()` is rewritten to `upsampled_count()` even though the query includes/excludes transactions, so `sum(sample_weight)` runs over events that have no sample weight and the reported count is wrong. The check needs to parse the filter rather than do a substring search (or at least exclude negated occurrences).

`errors` dataset enables `upsampled_count` but function is only registered in DiscoverDataset

`_should_apply_sample_weight_transform` returns True for `sentry.snuba.errors`, so `count()` is rewritten to `upsampled_count()` for `dataset=errors` requests. However the new `upsampled_count` SnQL function is only added to `DiscoverDataset.function_converter` (src/sentry/search/events/datasets/discover.py). If `ErrorsQueryBuilder`/the errors dataset resolves functions through a different converter that does not know `upsampled_count`, every errors-dataset stats request for an allowlisted org will fail with an unknown-function error at query time. Verify the errors dataset shares DiscoverDataset's function converter, or register `upsampled_count` there as well.

`sum(sample_weight)` silently drops events with NULL sample_weight

`upsampled_count` is defined as `toInt64(sum(sample_weight))`. ClickHouse `sum` ignores NULL inputs, so any event whose `sample_weight` is NULL is excluded from the count. The helper claims the schema guarantees `sample_weight` for all events (error_upsampling.py:85), but the only code populating it in this PR is gated on `contexts.error_sampling.client_sample_rate` (factories.py), i.e. only explicitly sampled events appear to have a weight. Events in an allowlisted project that were ingested without a client sample rate would have NULL `sample_weight` and vanish from the upsampled count, undercounting. Confirm the ingest pipeline writes a default weight of 1 for unsampled events, or use `sum(coalesce(sample_weight, 1))`.

Cache lookup and option read run for every stats request regardless of dataset

`is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects` builds the cache key and performs `cache.get` before checking whether the dataset is even relevant, and then still calls `_should_apply_sample_weight_transform` on a cache hit. `organization_events_stats` is a high-volume endpoint used for transactions/spans/logs, where the result is always discarded, so this adds a cache round-trip (and, on miss, an option read plus `cache.set`) to requests that can never use upsampling. Evaluate `_should_apply_sample_weight_transform(dataset, request)` first and only do the allowlist cache lookup when it is True.

`invalidate_upsampling_cache` is never called; stale eligibility after allowlist changes

`invalidate_upsampling_cache` documents that it must be called when the allowlist configuration changes, but nothing in this PR calls or wires it up. Changing `issues.client_error_sampling.project_allowlist` therefore leaves stale eligibility cached for up to 60s per org/project-set, so a newly allowlisted (or de-allowlisted) project keeps the old behavior until the TTL expires. Also note the contradictory documentation: `_are_all_projects_error_upsampled` says it always reads the allowlist fresh, while its caller caches the result for 60s. Either wire invalidation into the option-update path or remove the function and correct the docstrings.

Empty-allowlist branch is not actually tested

Under the comment 'Test when no projects are allowlisted' the test sets `mock_options.get.return_value = []` but then calls `_are_all_projects_error_upsampled([], self.organization)` with an empty project list. That returns False via the earlier `if not project_ids` guard, never reaching the `if not allowlist: return False` branch. The intended case (non-empty project ids with an empty allowlist) is therefore untested; pass `self.project_ids` instead of `[]` to exercise it.

true_positives.golden_comment: The Check operation exhibits asymmetric cache trust logic: cached permission grants are trusted and returned immediately, but cached denials from the same permission cache are ignored, leading to a fresh database lookup. This allows stale cached grants to provide access to revoked resources, posing a security risk.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Every resource absent from cached permissions now triggers a DB query

Before this change a Check for a resource not present in the user's cached permission map was answered from the cache (deny) without touching the database. Now, whenever the cached permission map exists but does not cover the requested resource, execution falls through to getIdentityPermissions, which always queries the permission store (the in-singleflight cache read was removed). The new denial cache only suppresses repeats of the exact same (user, action, name, parent) tuple, so workloads that check many distinct resources the user cannot access (a user or service account iterating/probing dashboards across an org) issue one DB query per distinct resource per 30s instead of being served from the permission cache. In large orgs this can significantly increase permission-store load.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments describe the exact same mechanism in the code: when checking permissions against the cache, a cache hit (grant) is returned immediately, while a cache miss/denial falls through to a fresh database lookup. While the golden comment frames this asymmetry primarily as a security risk (stale grants are trusted) and the candidate frames it as a performance issue (denials cause excessive DB queries), they both identify the same underlying flawed cache logic introduced by the change.

false_positives.candidate:
Denial cache key omits identity type, causing cross-identity denials

The new denial cache key is built only from the subject UID: userPermDenialCacheKey(ns, checkReq.UserUID, action, name, parent). It does not include checkReq.IdentityType nor the resolved user identifiers. Both 'anonymous:0' and 'render:0' carry UID "0", so a denied Check for an anonymous user (e.g. reading a private dashboard) stores a denial under the ..._0_... key, and the next render-service read Check for the same namespace/action/name/parent hits that entry and is incorrectly denied for up to 30s, breaking dashboard image rendering. The same key also collides when a subject is passed as a numeric user id (user:123) versus a user whose actual UID string is "123". The key must include the identity type (and should use the resolved user UID rather than the raw subject).

DB requery does not refresh the folder tree, so inherited access to new folders is still denied and cached

The new fallback only re-queries the user's permission scopes; it does not refresh the folder tree used by checkInheritedPermissions. buildFolderTree reads folderCache (shortCacheTTL = 30s) and nothing invalidates it when a folder is created. If the tree was cached before a new child folder was created, tree.Ancestors(parent) will not include the new folder, so a user whose access to the new folder/dashboard is inherited from an ancestor is denied even though permissions were re-queried. That false denial is then written to permDenialCache, keeping the user blocked for up to another 30s after the folder tree finally refreshes. This means the PR's stated target case (newly created folders) remains broken in any busy namespace where the folder tree is already cached.

Tests do not cover denial-cache writes or identity isolation

The new 'Should deny on explicit cache deny entry' test seeds permDenialCache by hand and only asserts the false result; it never exercises the code path that is supposed to populate the denial cache after a DB-backed denial, and it would still pass if the `s.permDenialCache.Set(...)` call at the end of Check were removed (the default fake store denies too). There is also no test that a denial cached for one identity type does not affect another, which is why the anonymous/"0" vs render/"0" collision above is not caught. Add a test that performs a denied Check and asserts the second call is served from the denial cache without a store call (e.g. via store.calls), and a test that a denial for anonymous:0 does not deny render:0.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The test comment says the cached permissions 'allow access', but the map stores false for dashboards:uid:dash1, so checkPermission will still treat this scope as not allowed.

The cache key construction in `userPermDenialCacheKey` uses simple string concatenation with underscores, which can lead to ambiguous keys and collision risks when any component contains underscores or is empty. This could result in incorrect denial cache hits, affecting user permissions.

true_positives.golden_comment: The GetWebAssets function implements an incomplete double-checked locking pattern for caching web assets. It also means a later reload that fails can overwrite an already-populated valid cache with nil, since `entryPointAssetsCache = result` is executed even on error. Re-check `cfg.Env != setting.Dev && entryPointAssetsCache != nil` immediately after taking the write lock (or use singleflight/double-checked locking) so only the first loader performs the work.

false_positives.candidate:
Async legacy writes are derived from the request context and get canceled when the request returns

In Create (line 51), Update (line 135), Delete (line 110) and DeleteCollection (line 163), the background goroutine derives its context via context.WithTimeoutCause(ctx, ...) from the ctx passed into the handler, which is the request-scoped context. The API server cancels the request context as soon as the response is written and the handler returns, so these goroutines will usually see context.Canceled almost immediately and the LegacyStorage call will abort before writing. This defeats the entire purpose of mode 3 (mirroring writes to the legacy store as a safety net): most legacy writes will silently never happen. Fix by detaching from cancellation, e.g. context.WithTimeoutCause(context.WithoutCancel(ctx), ...), while still carrying the logger values.

Storage failures are recorded as legacy durations

In Create the error branch calls d.recordLegacyDuration(true, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startStorage) even though the operation that just failed was the synchronous Storage.Create (and startStorage measures the storage call), so storage errors are attributed to the legacy-store metric. The same mistake exists in Update at line 129. Both should call recordStorageDuration with the storage timing. As-is, the storage error-rate/latency dashboards will be wrong and legacy error metrics will be inflated.

Async legacy write failures are never logged, so legacy drift is invisible

After writing to storage, the goroutines call the legacy store and only feed the error into d.recordLegacyDuration(...) (Create line 56, Update line 140, Delete line 113, DeleteCollection line 166). There is no log statement on failure, unlike the previous implementation which logged 'unable to create/update/delete ... in legacy storage'. Because the legacy write is the safety net for mode 3, a persistent failure (e.g. the context cancellation above, or a real legacy error) would silently cause the legacy store to diverge from unified storage with only a boolean counter to show it. Log the error, including the object name/kind, so operators can detect and repair drift.

Dual-write tests never wait for or assert the async legacy write, and share one mock for both stores

TestMode3_Create (line 65) and TestMode3_Update (line 345) return as soon as the synchronous storage call completes; the background legacy goroutine is not awaited and no assertion verifies LegacyStorage was actually called. Moreover the same *mock.Mock instance is used for both legacyStoreMock and storageMock, so even AssertCalled/AssertNotCalled cannot distinguish storage calls from legacy calls. The test therefore does not exercise the core behavior of mode 3 (async mirroring to the legacy store). The leaked goroutine can also touch the shared, non-thread-safe testify mock and the shared package-level prometheus registry after the subtest has finished, producing data races under -race. Use separate mocks and synchronize on the goroutine (e.g. a channel/WaitGroup injected for tests) before asserting.

Mode 3 playlist integration tests read the legacy API immediately after k8s writes and will be flaky

The added 'with dual write (... mode 3)' subtests (lines 132-144, 191-204, 287-312) run doPlaylistTests, which performs k8s CRUD and then immediately reads back via the legacy /api/playlists endpoints (e.g. the legacy list at line 523 and getFromBothAPIs at line 623) and asserts identical results. Under mode 3 the legacy write happens asynchronously, so the legacy store may not yet reflect the k8s create/update/delete when the legacy read runs, making require.Equal on the UID/field values intermittently fail. The tests need to wait/poll for the legacy mirror (or the shared helper must account for mode 3's asynchronous write semantics).

true_positives.matched_candidate:
Fallback chain mixes String and Symbol locales, defeating uniq and double-loading the YAML

`FallbackLocaleList#[]` builds `[locale, SiteSetting.default_locale.to_sym, :en]`. For anonymous requests `set_locale` assigns `I18n.locale = SiteSetting.default_locale`, which is a String, so `locale` is (for example) `"en"` while the site default is `:en`. `uniq` does not treat the String and Symbol as equal, so the chain becomes `["en", :en]`. Both values are then passed to `I18n.ensure_loaded!`, and because `@loaded_locales` stores them as distinct entries, `en.yml` is parsed twice on the first request and the same locale is translated twice inside the Fallbacks backend. Normalize the locale (e.g. `locale.to_sym`) when constructing the array.

The candidate points to one of the specific locations mentioned in the golden comment and provides the same recommendation (`locale.to_sym`).

The new `I18n.fallbacks.ensure_loaded!` call loads the user locale, the site default locale and `:en`, but it only runs inside `ApplicationController#set_locale`. Any translation performed outside a controller request — Sidekiq jobs, mailer/notification rendering, rake tasks, the console, specs — never executes it. In those contexts `I18n.translate` in `lib/freedom_patches/translate_accelerator.rb` still only calls `load_locale(config.locale)`, and the i18n `Fallbacks` backend invokes `Base#translate` (not `I18n.translate`) for each fallback, so it never triggers loading of the fallback locale files. Consequence: in a separate Sidekiq/mailer process, a key missing from, e.g., `de.yml` will not resolve to `:en` and will emit "translation missing" instead of falling back. The fallback-chain loading should live inside `I18n.translate`/`ensure_loaded!` rather than relying on the controller before_filter.

This change reworks how locale fallbacks are configured (dropping `config.i18n.fallbacks = true`, adding `FallbackLocaleList`, and adding `I18n.ensure_loaded!`) and directly affects user-visible output when translations are missing. No specs were added to verify that a key absent from a non-English locale resolves to the site default and then English, that `I18n.fallbacks.ensure_loaded!` actually loads the fallback locale files, or that pluralization still works through the fallback chain. Add request/unit coverage for these paths before merging, since a regression here silently produces "translation missing" strings.

`createInitialDeployment` returns early when `updateStrategy` is null, so `testImageChange(null)` and `testCacheMaxCount(null)` run against a CR that does not enable the `rolling-updates` feature. The docs added in this PR (advanced-configuration.adoc CAUTION) state the feature must be enabled or the Operator will fail, and `testCacheMaxCount(null)` expects a rolling update on a configuration change — behavior the flag is supposed to gate. Unless `getTestKeycloakDeployment(true)` already enables preview features, these two parameterized cases will either fail or silently exercise the un-gated path. If `getTestKeycloakDeployment(true)` returns a CR that already enables other features needed by the deployment (the null check implies a non-null FeatureSpec is possible), adding rolling-updates silently drops them and changes what the test actually deploys. true_positives.golden_comment: In getClientsWithPermission(String scope), iterating resourceStore.findByType(server, AdminPermissionsSchema.CLIENTS_RESOURCE_TYPE) and returning resource.getName() will only ever consider the type-level 'Clients' resource (per-client resources have no type) and return its name, while AvailableRoleMappingResource#getRoleIdsWithPermissions expects actual client IDs to pass to realm.getClientById, which can lead to incorrect behavior or a null client and subsequent failures.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
getClientsWithPermission cannot see per-client resources

`getClientsWithPermission` queries `resourceStore.findByType(server, CLIENTS_RESOURCE_TYPE, ...)`, but per-client resources created by `AdminPermissionsSchema.getOrCreateResource` are created with `resourceStore.create(server, name, owner)` and never assigned type `Clients`; only the all-clients resource created in `init` has that type. Consequently, when only per-client grants exist this method returns an empty set, and when an all-clients grant exists it adds the literal name `Clients` instead of actual client IDs. Callers that use the returned set to filter clients by per-client permission will see incorrect results. Either set the resource type when creating per-client resources or query them in another way.

Although it does not name the specific realm.getClientById caller or null-client failure, it correctly describes the cause and incorrect results.

Existing admin-permissions clients are not migrated to the new Clients resource type

Realms that already enabled ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2 before this change therefore never get the newly added `Clients` resource or the new scopes (`configure`, `map-roles-client-scope`, `map-roles-composite`). On such realms, creating a `Clients` scope permission later fails in `getOrCreateResource` because `scopeStore.findByName` returns null for the new scopes and throws `ModelException("No scopes found.")`. Code paths that look up the `Clients` all-resource also receive null. `init` must reconcile an existing admin-permissions client with the current schema instead of only creating it when absent.

Per-client resources hide global all-clients permissions

`hasPermission(ClientModel, scope)` looks up the client-specific resource and, when one exists, evaluates only that resource. It never evaluates the all-clients `Clients` resource in that case. A client-specific resource is created whenever any client-specific permission exists for that client, even if it belongs to a different admin. As a result, a user with global `manage`/`configure`/`view` on all clients can be denied access to a client merely because some unrelated client-specific permission exists for it; global deny policies can be bypassed in the same way. The evaluator must combine applicable permissions from both the per-client resource and the all-clients resource rather than treating the per-client resource as a complete replacement.

getGroupIdsWithViewPermission returns authorization resource IDs instead of group IDs

The set built by this method is consumed by UsersResource.searchForUser/getUsersCount and BruteForceUsersResource, which pass it into `UserModel.GROUPS`; the user store interprets those values as *group* IDs. This method adds `groupResource.getId()` (the internal authorization Resource UUID) and calls `hasPermission(groupResource.getId(), ...)`, which does `resourceStore.findByName(server, groupId)` — group resources are named by the group id (see AdminPermissionsSchema.resolveGroup), so passing the resource id makes the lookup miss and fall back to the shared 'Groups' resource. Existing admin-permissions clients never get the new Groups resource type and scopes

Existing third-party or downstream `CryptoProvider` implementations compiled against the previous `keycloak-common` do not implement it, and `CryptoIntegration.detectProvider()` now invokes `CryptoProvider::order` on every provider discovered via `ServiceLoader`. OrganizationAuditLogsEndpoint instantiates this paginator with order_by='-datetime', so self.key is 'datetime'. value_from_cursor returns a number for a datetime column, so subsequent pages filter incorrectly or fail

true_positives.golden_comment: A race condition in BuildIndex allows multiple goroutines to concurrently build the same expensive index for the same key. This is caused by moving the b.cacheMu lock from protecting the entire function to only protecting the final cache assignment.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Removing the BuildIndex lock allows concurrent duplicate builds of the same key and concurrent opens of the same on-disk index

BuildIndex no longer holds cacheMu while it creates/flushes the bleve index; the mutex is now only taken to assign b.cache[key] = idx at the end. Nothing else serializes builds per key: searchSupport.getOrCreateIndex calls GetIndex (returns nil), then both callers independently call s.build -> BuildIndex (this is also reached from handleEvent). Two concurrent callers therefore both create a bleve index, both run the full storage scan, and the later assignment silently overwrites the earlier cache entry, whose index is never closed (leak for mem-only indexes). The errgroup closures write to function-scoped shared state: `_, _, err = s.build(...)` assigns the outer `err`, and `totalBatchesIndexed++` mutates a shared counter. When the storage backend is stopped, the SQL backend's poller closes this channel (defer close(stream) in sql/backend.go), the receive yields a nil *WrittenEvent, and handleEvent immediately dereferences evt.Type -> nil-pointer panic that crashes the process; if the channel were not closed the loop would spin. init builds each index from storage and then calls s.storage.WatchWriteEvents, which for the SQL backend starts polling from the *latest* resource versions at subscription time. The per-index RV returned by s.build (the last RV read during the build) is discarded (`_, _, err = s.build(...)`), so any ADDED/MODIFIED/DELETED committed between the build snapshot and the watcher subscription is never applied to the index. The search index is then permanently stale for those resources (deleted documents keep matching, new documents are missing) until that resource is written again. The window is the whole startup index-build duration, so moving init to startup makes this easy to hit. The watch must start before/at the build RV (or events since that RV must be replayed) instead of from the current latest version.

This PR makes NewResourceServer run Init (lifecycle init, search index build via GetResourceStats/ListIterator, and WatchWriteEvents) synchronously during construction. The underlying failure should be fixed, or at minimum tracked by an issue referenced from the TODO, rather than silently skipping.

The most realistic trigger is `grouping_fn` (i.e. `ResultsStrategyFactory.build_payload_grouping_key`) raising on a malformed/partial result: that message is then discarded with only a log line and its offset is committed, bypassing any DLQ or retry. This differs from the batched/serial modes where a grouping failure propagates. The message should not be treated as successfully processed (e.g. add to DLQ / let the error propagate) rather than being committed away.

false_positives.candidate:
Changing span-buffer keys from sets to sorted sets breaks rolling deploys

Existing `span-buf:s:*` keys in Redis were written as sets by the previous `SADD`/`SSCAN` implementation. After a rolling deploy those keys can remain for the Redis TTL (default 3600s) and are still referenced by the flush queue, but the new code performs `ZADD` here and `ZSCAN`/`ZCARD`/`ZUNIONSTORE` elsewhere on them. Redis raises `WRONGTYPE Operation against a key holding the wrong kind of value`, so consumers and flushers fail and buffered spans can be lost. This needs a versioned key prefix, backward-compatible handling, or draining the buffer before deploy.

ZUNIONSTORE default SUM corrupts eviction scores for duplicate spans

`ZUNIONSTORE` without an aggregate uses `SUM`. Span processing is at-least-once, so after a span has been merged into a parent set, a retry can re-add the same payload to the source key; when the sets are merged again the member exists in both destination and source and its score is doubled. The score is `end_timestamp_precise`, so the `ZPOPMIN` eviction ordering is corrupted (an old span can look newer and survive eviction). The merge should preserve the original timestamp, e.g. with `AGGREGATE MAX`.

Eviction cap hardcodes 1000 and ignores max_segment_spans

The new eviction limit is hard-coded to 1000, while `SpansBuffer` still accepts `max_segment_spans` (default 1001) but no longer uses it. Deployments that configure a different limit are silently ignored, and spans beyond 1000 are dropped without any metric or log because the previous `segment_span_count_exceeded` signal was removed. This changes the configured data-loss boundary without visibility.

Redirect loop cap lowered to 1000 can misroute deep traces

The redirect-resolution loop was reduced from 10000 to 1000 iterations and the comment documenting the depth limitation was removed. For a project/trace chain longer than 1000 parent links, the loop stops at an intermediate span and writes the redirect to the wrong set, so spans can be merged into the wrong segment or split across segments. The redirect hash is not bounded by the 1000-span eviction cap until flush.

No test exercises the new eviction behavior

All test changes only add the new required `end_timestamp_precise` field to existing fixtures. There is no test that inserts more than 1000 spans to exercise the new `ZPOPMIN` cap, verifies that the oldest spans are evicted, or checks sorted-set merge behavior for duplicate payloads/scores. The main behavior added by this PR is therefore untested.

Denial cache key omits identity type, causing cross-identity denials

The new denial cache key is built only from the subject UID: userPermDenialCacheKey(ns, checkReq.UserUID, action, name, parent). It does not include checkReq.IdentityType nor the resolved user identifiers. Both 'anonymous:0' and 'render:0' carry UID "0", so a denied Check for an anonymous user (e.g. reading a private dashboard) stores a denial under the ..._0_... key, and the next render-service read Check for the same namespace/action/name/parent hits that entry and is incorrectly denied for up to 30s, breaking dashboard image rendering. The same key also collides when a subject is passed as a numeric user id (user:123) versus a user whose actual UID string is "123". The key must include the identity type (and should use the resolved user UID rather than the raw subject).

Every resource absent from cached permissions now triggers a DB query

Before this change a Check for a resource not present in the user's cached permission map was answered from the cache (deny) without touching the database. Now, whenever the cached permission map exists but does not cover the requested resource, execution falls through to getIdentityPermissions, which always queries the permission store (the in-singleflight cache read was removed). The new denial cache only suppresses repeats of the exact same (user, action, name, parent) tuple, so workloads that check many distinct resources the user cannot access (a user or service account iterating/probing dashboards across an org) issue one DB query per distinct resource per 30s instead of being served from the permission cache. In large orgs this can significantly increase permission-store load.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The regex pattern @(#{domains}) in email_in_restriction_setting? method only matches domain suffixes, not full domains with proper boundary anchoring. An attacker can register evil.example.com to bypass a whitelist entry for example.com.

true_positives.golden_comment: -webkit-box-ordinal-group and -moz-box-ordinal-group require values starting from 1, not 0. If $val is 0, this will cause incorrect rendering in older browsers, leading to layout issues.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
order mixin uses 0-based values for 1-based legacy flexbox property

The legacy flexbox properties -webkit-box-ordinal-group and -moz-box-ordinal-group use a 1-based initial value, while the standard order property uses 0. Emitting the same $val for both means the mixin does not provide equivalent behavior: for example @include order(1) has no effect in browsers using the legacy box syntax, and other values are shifted by one relative to modern flexbox. Since this mixin is intended to abstract ordering for the header layout, emit $val + 1 for the box-ordinal-group properties.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same bug: the mixin passes standard 0-based order values directly to legacy box-ordinal-group properties, which require 1-based values, causing incorrect ordering in older browsers.

false_positives.candidate:
Flex conversion of .small-action breaks right-aligned action button

Converting .small-action to a flex container invalidates the existing right-alignment mechanism: floats are ignored on flex items, so the button rule still using float: right no longer pushes the action to the right edge. At the same time .small-action-desc is not given flex: 1, so it shrink-wraps instead of consuming the row width. The result is that the button sits immediately after the description rather than at the far right, regressing the small-action row layout. Give .small-action-desc flex: 1 and/or give the button margin-left: auto.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Mixing float: left with flexbox causes layout issues. Further this PR removes the float-based right alignment for .d-header .panel, which may cause the login panel in the non-Ember/noscript header (where .panel is nested inside .row and not a flex item) to stack under the title instead of remaining right-aligned.
-ms-align-items never existed in any version of IE/Edge; the correct legacy property is -ms-flex-align.

true_positives.golden_comment: The include_website_name method is missing the required ? suffix. Rails serializers expect include_ methods to end with ? for conditional attribute inclusion, a convention followed by other methods in this serializer. Without it, the website_name attribute may not be conditionally included as intended. Additionally, the '.' << website_host string concatenation should be replaced with '.' + website_host or '.#{website_host}' to avoid mutating string literals, which can lead to issues.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
include_website_name is missing the trailing '?' so it never runs

ActiveModel::Serializer decides whether to emit an attribute by calling `include_<attribute>?`. This guard is named `include_website_name` (no trailing `?`), so it is never invoked and `website_name` is emitted for every serialized user, including users with no website (as `null`). The intended `website.present?` condition has no effect. Rename it to `include_website_name?`, or (better, see the trust-level finding) move `website_name` into `untrusted_attributes`.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same missing '?' suffix on include_website_name and its effect on conditional serialization. It does not mention the additional string-literal mutation concern, but it clearly matches the primary underlying issue.

false_positives.candidate:
website_name leaks a website that untrusted_attributes deliberately hides

`website` is listed in `untrusted_attributes` (lines 105-111) so that a TL0 user's profile fields are not exposed to anonymous visitors (`scope.restrict_user_fields?`). The new `website_name` attribute is added to the plain `attributes` list and has no such guard: its `include_website_name` method only checks `website.present?` and, being misnamed, is not called anyway. As a result anonymous visitors now receive `website_name` containing the hidden TL0 user's website host and path, defeating the anti-spam restriction. Add `:website_name` to `untrusted_attributes` (and make the include check honour `restrict_user_fields?`).

Gating the website block on model.website_name hides websites the serializer cannot parse

The block that renders the globe icon and the website link is now guarded by `{{#if model.website_name}}`. The serializer returns `nil` whenever `URI(website.to_s)` raises (e.g. a URL containing a space such as `http://example.com/my page`), and it is also absent if an endpoint does not include the new attribute. Previously the display name was derived in JS from `model.website` (`website.split('/')[2]`), so such a user still saw the globe and a link. Now the website silently disappears from the profile even though `model.website` is present. Gate on `model.website` and fall back to a derived name, or make the serializer always return a non-nil name when the website is present.

untested: website_name is not added to the untrusted attributes spec

The `untrusted_attributes` list still contains only the original attributes. Because `website_name` is not added, there is no test asserting that the new field is omitted for a TL0 user seen as anonymous, so the leak of a hidden website described elsewhere in this review passes the suite. Add `website_name` here; the test should fail until the serializer guards that attribute.

The equal-length subdomain branch of website_name is never exercised

The three new examples cover `website_host == discourse_host`, the `else` branch, and the parent-domain case. None exercises the `elsif` branch (`website_host.split('.').length == discourse_host.split('.').length && ... > 2`), i.e. the `www.example.com` vs `forum.example.com` case named in the code comment, which is the most complex branch. The nil/invalid-website case (host cannot be parsed) is also untested.

Subdomain comparison treats unrelated domains under multi-label public suffixes as equal

The equivalence check removes only the first label of each host and compares the rest. For hosts whose public suffix has more than one label this is wrong: with website `http://foo.co.uk/post` and instance `bar.co.uk`, comparing `['foo','co','uk'][1..-1].join` with `['bar','co','uk'][1..-1].join` yields `co.uk` for both, so it reports the domains as the same and shows the full path `foo.co.uk/post`, even though `foo.co.uk` and `bar.co.uk` are unrelated registrable domains. Use a real registrable-domain/public-suffix comparison, or only treat the website as a subdomain of the instance when it actually ends with `.` + instance host (and vice versa).

true_positives.golden_comment: The current origin validation using indexOf is insufficient and can be bypassed. An attacker could use a malicious domain like evil-discourseUrl.com to pass this check.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
postMessage origin check uses substring instead of exact origin

`discourseUrl.indexOf(e.origin) === -1` accepts any origin that appears as a substring of the configured Discourse URL. For example, with discourseUrl `http://example.com/`, an origin `http://example.co` passes, so another frame can send `discourse-resize` messages and alter the iframe height. Parse discourseUrl and compare the scheme/host/port exactly.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify insecure origin validation using indexOf/substring matching, allowing an attacker-controlled origin to pass instead of requiring an exact origin match. The differing bypass examples do not change the underlying issue.

true_positives.golden_comment: The TopicEmbed.import method is susceptible to a NoMethodError if the contents parameter is nil when attempting to append a string, and an XSS vulnerability due to unescaped url interpolation in the generated HTML.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
raw_html imports bypass sanitization and enable stored XSS

`Post#cook` returns `raw` unchanged when `cook_method` is `raw_html`, and `TopicEmbed.import` sets that for RSS/Readability content while `PollFeed` even calls `CGI.unescapeHTML` on it. `TopicEmbed.import` also interpolates the feed URL directly into an `<a href='...'>` footer. The imported HTML is stored unsanitized and `app/views/embed/best.html.erb:19` renders it with `raw post.cooked`. A feed containing `<script>`, event handlers, or `javascript:` URLs therefore executes in the Discourse origin. Sanitize the HTML before storing/serving it, or keep imported posts on the normal cook path.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate explicitly identifies the unescaped feed URL interpolation in TopicEmbed.import's HTML footer and its XSS risk, matching the golden comment's security issue. It does not mention the nil-contents NoMethodError, but captures the same underlying XSS bug.

true_positives.golden_comment: The ERB block closes with end if, which is invalid Ruby/ERB and will raise at render; it should just be end to close the if block.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
ERB `end if` is a syntax error and breaks the best view

The closing tag is `<%- end if %>` with no condition after `if`. ERB compiles this to invalid Ruby, so any request that renders the `best` template (i.e. whenever a TopicEmbed exists) raises a template error/500 instead of showing the embedded discussion. The closing tag should be `<%- end %>`.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the invalid ERB closing statement `end if`, explain that it causes a render-time syntax error, and recommend replacing it with `end`.

true_positives.golden_comment: Calling `i.content.scrub` assumes that `i.content` is always populated. However, many RSS feeds do not provide a `content` field, leading to a potential nil pointer exception when `i.content` is nil. A fallback to `description` should be implemented to prevent crashes.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
PollFeed assumes every RSS item has `content`

`i.content` is not defined for standard RSS items that only provide `<description>` or `<summary>`. Calling `.scrub` on nil raises NoMethodError, and because PollFeed has retry disabled a single such item aborts the hourly polling run so later items are never imported. Use a fallback such as `i.content || i.description` and guard against nil.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify that RSS items may lack content, causing i.content.scrub to fail on nil, and recommend falling back to description to prevent crashes.

false_positives.candidate:
Updating a TopicEmbed whose post was deleted raises and stops feed polling

When an existing embed is found, `post = embed.post` is used without checking whether the post still exists. If the imported topic/post was deleted, `embed.post` can be nil; on a content change `PostRevisor.new(post).revise!` then dereferences nil and raises, aborting the whole PollFeed run (retry is disabled). Remove or repair stale TopicEmbed rows before revising.

Open-uri fetch follows redirects and permits SSRF

`open(url).read` performs an unrestricted outbound request. The only host validation, `TopicRetriever#invalid_host?`, checks the original URI host; `open-uri` follows redirects, so an allowed embeddable host that has an open redirect can make the Discourse server fetch localhost/internal services or cloud metadata and then import the response into a post. Validate redirect targets and block private addresses, and add timeouts/size limits.

Success spec leaves @topic_view nil and cannot pass

`TopicView.expects(:new).with(...)` has no `.returns(...)`, so the controller assigns nil to @topic_view. The rendered `best` view immediately calls `@topic_view.posts` and raises NoMethodError, so the after block expecting a successful response fails. Stub TopicView.new to return a view object with a topic and posts.

PollFeed guard tests are vacuous

The tests for missing feed_polling_url and missing embed_by_username do not stub feed_polling_enabled? to true, and the default is false. The execute condition therefore short-circuits before reaching the setting under test, so these specs pass even if the URL/username guards are removed. Stub the other required settings to true.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The PollFeed job calls open(SiteSetting.feed_polling_url) without validating the URL, allowing an attacker who controls the feed_polling_url site setting to make the server fetch arbitrary internal or external URLs.
postMessage targetOrigin should be the origin (scheme+host+port), not the full referrer URL; using the full URL will cause the message to be dropped and prevent resizing.

The code sets X-Frame-Options: ALLOWALL which completely disables clickjacking protection. The referer validation can be bypassed (referer headers are easily spoofed), and the fallback to empty string for nil referer masks validation failures.

An unescaped request header (request.referer) is interpolated into JavaScript without proper escaping, which can lead to XSS vulnerabilities if the referer contains malicious content. This issue can allow attackers to execute arbitrary scripts in the context of the application.

true_positives.golden_comment: The downsize method is defined twice. The second definition, which expects a single dimensions string parameter, overrides the first, which expected separate max_width and max_height parameters. This makes the original method unreachable and breaks existing code that calls it with separate width and height arguments.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Second `downsize` definition silently replaces the width/height overload

The file now defines `self.downsize` twice: the pre-existing `downsize(from, to, max_width, max_height, opts={})` at line 145 and the newly added `downsize(from, to, dimensions, opts={})` at line 149. Ruby keeps only the last definition, so the four-argument form quietly disappears. Existing callers using `OptimizedImage.downsize(from, to, width, height)` will bind `height` to `opts`, and `optimize` later evaluates `opts[:allow_animation]` on an Integer, raising NoMethodError; callers passing five arguments raise ArgumentError. This is a public class-method contract break and will also break any existing specs. Remove or rename one overload (or dispatch on argument count) and update callers.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify that the second downsize definition overrides the original width/height signature, making it unreachable and breaking existing callers that pass separate width and height arguments.

true_positives.golden_comment: Hardcoding maxSizeKB = 10 * 1024 ignores Discourse.SiteSettings['max_' + type + '_size_kb'], so the client-side limit can diverge from server-side and per-type settings (also applies to the 413 handler below).
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Hardcoded 10MB client limit ignores per-type site settings

Both client-side checks were changed from `Discourse.SiteSettings['max_' + type + '_size_kb']` (and `max_image_size_kb` in the 413 handler at line 246) to a hardcoded `10 * 1024`. This raises the client-side limit for attachments to 10MB regardless of `max_attachment_size_kb`, so files the admin disallowed pass validation and are sent to the server. For images, an admin who configures `max_image_size_kb` above 10MB now sees valid uploads rejected, while an unlimited (0) setting is effectively capped at 10MB. The 10MB constant is duplicated in the 413 handler, so the two can drift. Use the site setting, or `max(setting, 10MB)` only for images, and share a single constant.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the hardcoded 10MB limit replacing per-type site settings, causing client-side validation to diverge from configured server limits, including in the 413 handler.

true_positives.golden_comment: Passing 80% as the dimensions can fail for animated GIFs when allow_animated_thumbnails is true, since the animated path uses gifsicle --resize-fit which expects WxH geometry, not a percentage; downsizing would then silently fail.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Animated GIF downsize passes a percentage to gifsicle

This call passes dimensions `"80%"` together with `allow_animation: SiteSetting.allow_animated_thumbnails`. When `optimize` selects the animated path (for a `from` path ending in `.GIF`), `downsize_instructions_animated` delegates to `resize_instructions_animated`, which builds `gifsicle ... --resize-fit 80% ...`. gifsicle's `--resize-fit` expects a `WxH` value, not a percentage, so the command fails, the loop burns all five attempts, and the oversized GIF is uploaded unchanged. If the temp path does not end in `.GIF`, the animated branch is not selected at all. Pass pixel dimensions (or use the percentage only with `convert`), and ensure the animated path is actually selected for browser uploads.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same issue: passing "80%" to the animated GIF path produces a gifsicle --resize-fit argument that requires WxH geometry, causing downsizing to fail when animated thumbnails are allowed. The additional path-selection concern does not change the core match.

false_positives.candidate:
Downsize loop ignores failures and proceeds with an oversized or corrupt file

`OptimizedImage.downsize` returns `false` when the ImageMagick/gifsicle command fails or the output cannot be written, but the loop ignores the return value and merely decrements `attempt`. After five failures it exits and `Upload.create_for` is called with the original tempfile, so an image still larger than `max_image_size_kb` (or a partially written file) can be persisted as an upload, with no error returned to the user. There is also no final size check after the loop. Check the downsize result/final size and reject with a clear error instead of silently storing the oversized file.

API download cap hardcoded to 10MB, ignoring configured limits

`FileHelper.download(url, 10.megabytes, ...)` replaces the configured limit with a fixed 10MB. If `max_image_size_kb` or the attachment limit is configured higher than 10MB, permitted API uploads now fail; if configured lower, the server will download and store files larger than the site's limit (non-images are never downsized). The same 10MB value is also duplicated in the JavaScript client, so client and server limits can silently diverge. Derive the download limit from the relevant site setting, with the 10MB floor only if that is the intended behavior for images.

No tests for the new auto-downsize behavior

The PR adds non-trivial branching (image vs non-image, successful downsize, downsize failure, animated GIFs, oversized files, API url uploads) without any specs. Tests exercising these paths would have caught the overridden `downsize` signature and the invalid `gifsicle --resize-fit 80%` command. Add coverage for `create_upload` downsize behavior and the new `downsize(from, to, dimensions)` overload.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The loop checking `tempfile.size` may never terminate correctly due to stale cached size, leading to potential infinite loops or incorrect file handling after modifications.

true_positives.golden_comment: logic: Potential nil pointer exception - if no TopicUser record exists, tu will be nil and calling methods on it will crash
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Unsubscribe crashes when the user has no TopicUser row

`TopicUser.find_by` can return nil, but the action immediately calls `tu.notification_level` and later `tu.save!`. A logged-in user hitting `/t/:slug/:id/unsubscribe` for a topic they have never visited, or whose TopicUser row has been removed, gets a NoMethodError/500 instead of an unsubscribe. Use `TopicUser.change` (which creates the row and publishes the level change) or handle nil explicitly.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same nil dereference: when no TopicUser record exists, tu is nil, and calling methods on it causes a crash.

false_positives.candidate:
Unsubscribe is a state-changing GET with no signed token

The new route is a plain GET that calls `TopicsController#unsubscribe`, which changes the logged-in user's `topic_users.notification_level`. Because the URL has no signed per-recipient token and GET requests are not CSRF-protected, any third-party page can embed/fetch this URL for a logged-in user and silently mute or downgrade notifications for a topic; mail scanners/link prefetchers can trigger the same effect. Use a signed token and/or a POST/confirmation flow for the mutation.

Repeated unsubscribe requests progressively downgrade the topic

The new level depends on the current level: watching/tracking becomes regular, while regular/muted becomes muted. A page refresh, double-click, or a fetched-link retry therefore runs the mutation again and can take a user from watching to regular and then to muted. The unsubscribe target should be deterministic/idempotent (or encoded in a signed link), otherwise retries silently over-mute the topic.

unsubscribe_link now requires unsubscribe_url for every add_unsubscribe_link email

The shared server locale string now interpolates `%{unsubscribe_url}`. `Email::MessageBuilder` still treats `unsubscribe_url` as optional and only checks `add_unsubscribe_link` when rendering `I18n.t('unsubscribe_link', template_args)`. Any caller using `add_unsubscribe_link: true` without the new option, or a non-topic/digest mailer that only supplies `user_preferences_url`, will raise `I18n::MissingInterpolationArgument` and fail to build the email. Default `unsubscribe_url` to the preferences URL, guard the interpolation, or keep the per-topic sentence in a separate conditional string.

No coverage for the new unsubscribe endpoint or per-topic link

The PR adds a destructive controller action and URL but the only spec change adds an unused `unsubscribe_url` to an existing email-builder test. There are no tests that the per-topic URL appears in the email body, that `TopicsController#unsubscribe` updates `notification_level` correctly (including when no TopicUser exists), or that repeated requests do not further downgrade the setting. Add request/controller specs so these behaviors are protected.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Typo in property name: 'stopNotificiationsText' should be 'stopNotificationsText' (missing 'n' in 'Notifications')

true_positives.golden_comment: logic: macOS-specific sed syntax with empty string after -i flag will fail on Linux systems
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Webhook test script uses macOS-only sed syntax

`sed -i '' -E ...` is BSD/macOS syntax. GNU sed on Linux interprets the empty string incorrectly and fails or behaves unpredictably, so the script cannot update `.env` on Linux. Separately, `ENV_FILE` on line 5 is relative to the caller’s current working directory, so running it from the repo root writes to the parent directory’s `.env` rather than the repo `.env`. Use a portable in-place edit and resolve paths relative to the script location.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate explicitly identifies the same macOS/BSD-specific `sed -i ''` syntax failing on Linux with GNU sed. The additional path concern does not negate the match.

true_positives.golden_comment: Date is formatted with hardcoded 'en-US' locale instead of using the user's locale from useLocale, which can lead to incorrect date representation for users in different locales.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Cache timestamp is hard-coded to en-US

The component formats `cacheUpdatedAt` with `new Intl.DateTimeFormat("en-US", ...)`, ignoring the active locale from `useLocale`. Users in other locales get U.S.-formatted dates in an otherwise localized UI. Use the current locale or a shared date formatting helper instead of the literal `"en-US"`.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same issue: date formatting hardcodes "en-US" instead of using the active locale from useLocale, resulting in incorrect locale-specific date representation.

false_positives.candidate:
Cache status includes expired cache rows

`getCacheStatusByCredentialIds` aggregates every `CalendarCache` row for the credential without filtering on `expiresAt`, while `getCachedAvailability` only serves rows with `expiresAt >= now`. Expired rows are not deleted elsewhere, so `cacheUpdatedAt` stays non-null after the cache expires. The UI then shows “Cache Status / Last updated” and “Delete cached data” for a cache that is not actually being served, giving users a misleading view of cache state. Add an `expiresAt: { gte: new Date() }` predicate or return expiry state explicitly.

Migration backfills every cache row with the deployment time

Adding `updatedAt ... DEFAULT NOW()` sets all pre-existing `CalendarCache` rows to the time the migration runs. Since the new UI displays `_max(updatedAt)` as “Last updated”, every existing cached credential will appear to have been refreshed at deploy time even though the old rows have no real update timestamp. Existing caches will report a false freshness date until each row is rewritten. Consider making the column nullable for legacy rows, backfilling from a meaningful source, or suppressing the status for backfilled rows.

Cache deletion does not invalidate connected calendars query

`deleteCacheMutation` only calls the optional `onSuccess` callback. Unlike `disconnectMutation`, it never invalidates `viewer.calendars.connectedCalendars`, and `onSuccess` is optional at this component’s API. In a caller that does not pass an invalidating `onSuccess`, the dropdown continues to render the old `cacheUpdatedAt` timestamp and a delete action for data that no longer exists until the user manually refreshes. Invalidate `utils.viewer.calendars.connectedCalendars` after successful deletion.

No tests for destructive cache deletion authorization

This PR adds a destructive `deleteCache` mutation and an ownership check, but no tests cover the new handler, the unauthorized path (credential id belonging to another user), or the repository’s `getCacheStatusByCredentialIds` behavior (empty ids, multiple cache rows, expired rows). A regression in the ownership check would let a user delete another user’s cache. Add unit/integration tests for authorized and unauthorized deletion and the cache-status query.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The updateManyByCredentialId call uses an empty data object, which prevents Prisma's @updatedAt decorator from updating the updatedAt timestamp. This results in inaccurate cache status tracking, as the timestamp isn't updated when the cache is refreshed. To fix this, explicitly set the updatedAt field.

Throwing a generic Error for authentication failures results in a 500 response in tRPC. Instead, it should return a structured TRPCError with an appropriate code, such as FORBIDDEN, to accurately reflect the error type.

true_positives.golden_comment: Incorrect end time calculation using slotStartTime instead of slotEndTime
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Slot end is never checked against working-hour end

`end` is computed from `slotStartTime.hour()` and `slotStartTime.minute()` instead of `slotEndTime`, so `end > workingHour.endTime` can never detect a slot extending past the working hours when the start is inside the range. In a round-robin event with a fixed host whose availability ends before the event slot's end, a 60-minute slot starting at 10:30 passes a working-hour range ending at 11:00. This should use the slot end time for the upper-bound check.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate explicitly identifies that end is calculated from slotStartTime instead of slotEndTime, matching the golden comment's underlying bug.

true_positives.golden_comment: Using === for dayjs object comparison will always return false as it compares object references, not values. Use .isSame() method instead: dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, 'minutes').isSame(dayjs(date.end).add(utcOffset, minutes))
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Zero-length date override check compares Dayjs objects by identity

The condition `dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, "minutes") === dayjs(date.end).add(utcOffset, "minutes")` compares two separate Dayjs object instances and is always false. A date override with identical start and end, which is the representation this code is trying to treat as a fully unavailable day, is not handled; for a slot starting exactly at the override start, the other boundary checks also fail to reject it, so a slot can leak through. Use `.isSame()` or compare timestamps.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same bug: strict equality compares separate Dayjs object references rather than their date values, making the condition always false. Both recommend using .isSame().

false_positives.candidate:
Date override path skips busy-time checks

`checkIfIsAvailable` now returns `true` as soon as a date override exists for the slot's day and the slot is not completely outside it, before reaching the `busy.every(...)` check. Existing bookings or calendar busy times that fall inside a date override are therefore ignored when filtering fixed/loose hosts. A host with an override 10:00-11:00 and a booking 10:00-10:30 will still be offered at 10:00, allowing a double booking. The override check should only decide whether the slot is within the override; busy-time filtering must still run afterward.

Partially overlapping slots are accepted for date overrides

The override containment logic only rejects a slot when it ends at/before the override start or starts strictly after the override end. A slot that starts before the override and ends inside it is treated as available, and a slot starting exactly at the override end is also accepted because the final condition uses `isAfter(end)` instead of also rejecting `isSame(end)`. For example, with a fixed host override 10:00-11:00 and an event slot 09:30-10:30 generated from another host, the fixed host check passes even though the fixed host is only available 10:00-11:00. The slot should be available only when `slotStartTime >= overrideStart` and `slotEndTime <= overrideEnd`.

Working-hours check rejects valid split availability

The working-hours validation uses `find` with a callback that returns true when the slot is outside that particular working-hour range. If a host has two same-day ranges, e.g. 09:00-12:00 and 13:00-17:00, a 10:00 slot is rejected because the second range returns true when `start < workingHour.startTime`. Since this check runs for fixed hosts and personal-event users, split availability becomes largely unavailable. The code should use `some`/`every` to reject only when no same-day range contains the slot.

Date override day filter ignores converted invitee date

`activeOverrides` still filters by comparing the organizer's original `override.start` against `startOfInviteeDay`, without applying the timezone offset computed below. This breaks date overrides when the converted time falls on a different invitee day. Example: 09:30-18:00 Asia/Kolkata on Aug 15 is 21:00 Aug 14-04:30 Aug 15 in America/Los_Angeles, but the override is not active for the invitee Aug 14 day; it is instead applied one day later on Aug 15. The filter needs to use the same converted instant as the minute calculation.

No test covers round-robin fixed-host date overrides

The only added test checks a personal event with a +30 minute timezone difference, where the override stays on the same invitee day. It does not cover the PR's main behavior: a round-robin event with a fixed host date override, a negative timezone offset/day rollover, or a date override combined with an existing busy booking. The new `checkIfIsAvailable` override/working-hours logic is therefore untested for the cases most likely to regress, including skipping busy times or accepting partially overlapping slots.

true_positives.golden_comment: Using retryCount: reminder.retryCount + 1 reads a possibly stale value and can lose increments under concurrency; consider an atomic increment via Prisma (increment: 1) to avoid race conditions (also applies to the similar update in the catch block).
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Retry count increment is a lost-update race

A backup code must not replace the password factor; verify the password whenever backupCode is supplied, or explicitly validate only the selected factor while still requiring the password.

Closing backup-codes screen via dialog X skips onEnable and loses codes

After `handleEnable` succeeds, 2FA is already enabled on the server and the modal switches to `DisplayBackupCodes`. Only the explicit Close button calls `onEnable()` and `resetState()`. Closing via the dialog's X, Escape, or outside click calls `onOpenChange` directly, so the settings switch is not updated, the component can reopen on the stale backup-codes step, and the user may leave without ever seeing or saving the only copy of the backup codes. Any dismissal while on `DisplayBackupCodes` should either commit the enable state and reset state, or be blocked until the user confirms they have saved the codes.

No coverage for actual backup-code login, consumption, or disable flow

The added e2e assertions only check that the download has the expected filename and that a copy-success toast appears; the file contents and clipboard contents are explicitly left as TODO. There is no test that logs in with a backup code, rejects an invalid code, verifies a used code cannot be reused, or disables 2FA using a backup code. These are the security-critical paths added by this PR, and a regression in code formatting, one-time consumption, or either server endpoint would currently pass the tests.

Copy button shows success toast even when clipboard write fails

`navigator.clipboard.writeText(...)` returns a promise that can reject when clipboard permission is denied or the API is unavailable, but the promise is neither awaited nor caught and the success toast is shown unconditionally. Users can be told the backup codes were copied when nothing was copied, or an unhandled rejection can be produced. Await the clipboard write and show the success toast only after it resolves, with an error fallback.

Password visibility toggle is ineffective after switching to PasswordField

`PasswordField` sets its own `type` based on `isPasswordVisible` before spreading `{...props}`, so passing `type="password"` here overrides that dynamic value. Clicking the eye button changes the visibility state but the input remains `type="password"`, making the newly added visibility control non-functional in the enable-2FA modal. Remove the explicit `type` prop when using `PasswordField`, or change `PasswordField` so caller props cannot override its visibility-driven type.

Password visibility toggle removed from keyboard navigation

Adding `tabIndex={-1}` to the password visibility button removes it from the keyboard tab order. Keyboard-only users can no longer focus the control to reveal or re-hide the password, which is an accessibility regression for every `PasswordField` in the application. Keep the button focusable, or provide an equivalent keyboard-accessible way to toggle visibility.

isinstance guard prevents killing spawn-context flusher processes

In `_ensure_processes_alive` the call `process.kill()` is now guarded by `isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process)`. On Linux, `multiprocessing.Process` resolves to the default (fork) class `ForkProcess`, while these flusher workers are created with `multiprocessing.get_context("spawn").Process`, i.e. `SpawnProcess`. `SpawnProcess` is a sibling of `ForkProcess` (both subclass `BaseProcess`), not a subclass of it, so this check is False and `kill()` never runs. As a result a dead or hung worker is never terminated before a replacement is spawned: dead children become zombies (never reaped) and hung children keep running and flushing the same shards concurrently with the new worker, leading to duplicate/partial writes to `buffered-segments`. The pre-PR code called `self.process.kill()` unconditionally (with a `ValueError` catch), so this is a regression. The same guard at line 346 also means `terminate()` in `join()` never fires for spawn processes. true_positives.golden_comment: A race condition in BuildIndex allows multiple goroutines to concurrently build the same expensive index for the same key. This is caused by moving the b.cacheMu lock from protecting the entire function to only protecting the final cache assignment.

Nothing else serializes builds per key: searchSupport.getOrCreateIndex calls GetIndex (returns nil), then both callers independently call s.build -> BuildIndex (this is also reached from handleEvent). Two concurrent callers therefore both create a bleve index, both run the full storage scan, and the later assignment silently overwrites the earlier cache entry, whose index is never closed (leak for mem-only indexes). For keys above FileThreshold both goroutines call bleve.New on the same directory concurrently, which bleve/bolt does not support and can fail or corrupt the on-disk index. The previous global lock serialized these builds; if it is removed, a per-key lock/singleflight is required (the TODO in getOrCreateIndex explicitly notes this is missing).
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate describes the same issue as the golden comment. The cacheMu lock now covers only the final cache assignment instead of the whole BuildIndex function, so multiple goroutines can concurrently build the same index for the same key.

false_positives.candidate:

The errgroup closures write to function-scoped shared state: `_, _, err = s.build(...)` assigns the outer `err`, and `totalBatchesIndexed++` mutates a shared counter. With group.SetLimit(s.initWorkers) and WorkerThreads > 1 these closures run concurrently, so this is a data race (will be reported by -race). Consequences: the error returned by a closure can be a value written by another goroutine (wrong error propagation), and the 'namespaced_indexed' span attribute is racy/incorrect. Use a closure-local error (`_, _, buildErr := ...; return buildErr`) and an atomic (or per-goroutine) counter.

Watch-event consumer dereferences a nil event when the events channel is closed, panicking on shutdown

The goroutine started by searchSupport.init does `v := <-events; s.handleEvent(watchctx, v)` without checking the receive ok flag and without ever exiting. When the storage backend is stopped, the SQL backend's poller closes this channel (defer close(stream) in sql/backend.go), the receive yields a nil *WrittenEvent, and handleEvent immediately dereferences evt.Type -> nil-pointer panic that crashes the process; if the channel were not closed the loop would spin. Additionally the goroutine uses context.Background() and has no way to be stopped. Because this PR makes searchSupport.init run unconditionally during construction, this goroutine (and the shutdown panic) is now always started. Check the comma-ok receive and return when the channel is closed.

Writes committed between index build and watch subscription are dropped permanently by searchSupport.init

init builds each index from storage and then calls s.storage.WatchWriteEvents, which for the SQL backend starts polling from the *latest* resource versions at subscription time. The per-index RV returned by s.build (the last RV read during the build) is discarded (`_, _, err = s.build(...)`), so any ADDED/MODIFIED/DELETED committed between the build snapshot and the watcher subscription is never applied to the index. The search index is then permanently stale for those resources (deleted documents keep matching, new documents are missing) until that resource is written again. The window is the whole startup index-build duration, so moving init to startup makes this easy to hit. The watch must start before/at the build RV (or events since that RV must be replayed) instead of from the current latest version.

Skipping the postgres variant of the storage-server integration test removes the only DB-backed coverage of the new startup path

This PR makes NewResourceServer run Init (lifecycle init, search index build via GetResourceStats/ListIterator, and WatchWriteEvents) synchronously during construction. That is exactly the path the storage-server-target integration test exercises, and postgres is the only real database variant left after sqlite is already skipped. Adding a skip with a TODO hides whatever failure the change introduces (e.g. unified-storage tables/migrations not being available when the resource server is constructed, or a startup error/hang) and leaves zero postgres coverage for the storage server target. The underlying failure should be fixed, or at minimum tracked by an issue referenced from the TODO, rather than silently skipping.

The score is `end_timestamp_precise`, so the `ZPOPMIN` eviction ordering is corrupted (an old span can look newer and survive eviction). The merge should preserve the original timestamp, e.g. with `AGGREGATE MAX`.

The new eviction limit is hard-coded to 1000, while `SpansBuffer` still accepts `max_segment_spans` (default 1001) but no longer uses it. Deployments that configure a different limit are silently ignored, and spans beyond 1000 are dropped without any metric or log because the previous `segment_span_count_exceeded` signal was removed. This changes the configured data-loss boundary without visibility.

Redirect loop cap lowered to 1000 can misroute deep traces

The redirect-resolution loop was reduced from 10000 to 1000 iterations and the comment documenting the depth limitation was removed. For a project/trace chain longer than 1000 parent links, the loop stops at an intermediate span and writes the redirect to the wrong set, so spans can be merged into the wrong segment or split across segments. The redirect hash is not bounded by the 1000-span eviction cap until flush.

No test exercises the new eviction behavior

All test changes only add the new required `end_timestamp_precise` field to existing fixtures. There is no test that inserts more than 1000 spans to exercise the new `ZPOPMIN` cap, verifies that the oldest spans are evicted, or checks sorted-set merge behavior for duplicate payloads/scores. The main behavior added by this PR is therefore untested.

That false denial is then written to permDenialCache, keeping the user blocked for up to another 30s after the folder tree finally refreshes. false_positives.candidate:
Member list is rendered with an invalid each helper

The new member-list block is written as `{{each member in members itemView='group-member'}}` without the leading `#` and there is no closing `{{/each}}`. Handlebars treats this as an inline helper, not a block, so the group-member template is never rendered; the admin group member list and its remove links are missing or rendering fails. Use `{{#each member in members itemView='group-member'}} ... {{/each}}`.

Removing the last member on the last page leaves an empty member list

`findMembers` clamps the requested offset with `Math.min(user_count, ...)`. If an admin removes the only member on the last page, user_count falls to the current offset (for example 50), so the reload requests offset=50 against a 50-member total and receives an empty array. The member list goes blank; clamp to the last valid page start or step back a page when offset >= user_count.

Public group members endpoint now silently truncates at 50 with no public pagination

The endpoint now defaults to limit 50, but the public group/members route and template have no pagination or load-more control. Public group pages therefore silently show only the first 50 members; before this change manual groups returned all members and automatic groups up to 200. Add pagination to the public page or avoid applying the 50-row default there. The supplied limit is also not capped, so callers can request arbitrarily large pages.

Member reload uses the unsaved editable group name

`findMembers` builds the URL from `this.get('name')`, but the admin form edits `name` directly. If an admin renames a group and then adds/removes a member or pages before saving, the add/remove request uses the id and succeeds, but the follow-up GET uses the unsaved new name and fails or returns 404, leaving the member list stale. Use the group id for admin member listing or the persisted name.

Remove link is shown for automatic groups because automatic is read from the wrong context

This template is the itemView for each member, so its context is the member rather than the parent group. `automatic` is a group attribute and is undefined in this scope, making `unless automatic` true; the remove link is shown even for automatic groups. Removing then fails with a 422. Pass the group's automatic flag into the item view or render the link conditionally from the parent template.

Creating a group ignores the submitted alias_level

`create` only assigns name and visible. `Group#asJSON` includes alias_level, and the form allows choosing it for a new group, so the submitted alias_level is silently ignored and the new group keeps the default until an explicit update. Assign alias_level in create (with the same presence check used in update).

true_positives.golden_comment: BlockedEmail.should_block_email? method has side effects during a read operation - it updates statistics even when just checking if an email should be blocked. This could cause race conditions in concurrent environments and makes the method name misleading.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
should_block? mutates the record during validation and is not atomic

`BlockedEmail.should_block?` performs `record.match_count += 1` and `record.save` every time it is called, but it is called from `EmailValidator`, so it runs during validation rather than only when a signup actually fails. In `UsersController#create`, `user.valid?` (line 168) is followed by `user.save` (line 172), so a single blocked signup attempt invokes it twice and increments `match_count` twice; any other `valid?` call also increments it. The read/modify/write is also racy, so concurrent checks lose increments. This makes `match_count`/`last_match_at` unreliable and adds database writes to validation. Record the match once at the point of the blocked signup, and use an atomic counter update such as `increment_counter`/`update_counters`.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments describe the same problem. The method that checks whether an email should be blocked also updates match statistics as a side effect. Both flag that this read/modify/write is racy under concurrency. The candidate adds the double-increment caused by calling validation twice, but the core issue is identical.

true_positives.golden_comment: The case-sensitive email lookup in `BlockedEmail.should_block?` creates a bypass risk, allowing 'User@Example.com' to bypass a block on 'user@example.com'. This can lead to unauthorized access to blocked users.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Blocked-email lookup is case- and whitespace-sensitive, allowing bypass

`BlockedEmail.should_block?` looks up the raw submitted value with `BlockedEmail.where(email: email).first`, and `set_defaults` never normalizes stored addresses. On the default Postgres setup this comparison is case-sensitive, and surrounding whitespace also matters. A blocked address such as `spammer@example.com` can therefore still register as `Spammer@example.com` or `spammer@example.com ` because the validator finds no record and returns false. Normalize both the stored address and the lookup value (for example with `Email.downcase`/strip), and enforce that normalization on write, including the unique constraint, so the block cannot be bypassed by casing or whitespace.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments describe the same bug: the case-sensitive email lookup in BlockedEmail.should_block? lets a blocked address get through when it is submitted with different casing. The candidate also mentions whitespace, but the core issue is the same.
